sheet-2.description: Sheet 2 shows the business centre of Washington borough, where West and East Washington Avenue meet Belvidere Avenue and Broad Street at the middle of the sheet. The sheet is turned so that north points toward the upper left; Church Street runs up the left margin and North Lincoln Avenue and South Lincoln Avenue form the bottom edge. West Washington Avenue climbs from the Lincoln Avenue line to the central junction and continues as East Washington Avenue toward the top right, lined on both sides with continuous blocks of brick stores in pink and frame buildings in yellow. Notable buildings include the Borough Hall and fire department with its hose tower and jail on Belvidere Avenue, the First National Bank building, the Washington Opera House with a movie theatre, the Bakers Inn, the Post Office, the St. Cloud Hotel and St. Cloud Theatre, a printing office, a garage and repair shop, a library and school office near the top, and the large Cornish Co. piano and phonograph works with its dry kilns and steel water tower along the bottom. Residential lots with detached dwellings occupy the left margin along Church Street and the lower right along Broad Street. Water pipes are lettered along the principal streets, with hydrants and the sizes of the mains. A compass rose, the sheet's scale bar (50 ft to an inch, graduated to 150 ft) and the date stamp for June 1924 are printed on the right side. Shabecong Creek, crossed by a bridge, forms the lower right corner. Neighbouring sheets are 3, 4, 5, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14 and 15, whose numbers are printed in the margins.
notes: Church Street here is today West Church Street and East Church Street; Washington Avenue is West and East Washington Avenue; Broad is Broad Street.

The junction of Belvidere Avenue, Broad Street and Washington Avenue is a single node in OpenStreetMap; the sheet draws Belvidere Avenue and Broad Street meeting Washington Avenue at slightly different places.
Cherry Street and Madison Street are drawn about 20 ft wide and were left out of the control points.
East Church Street / Taylor Street is a hand-picked control point (the street leaves the sheet, so the detector could not measure it).
School is lettered along the street at the top of the sheet (medium confidence that it is a street name rather than a building label).
50 ft. Business centre (Washington Av E/W, Broad, Belvidere Av, Church, Lincoln Av), drawn turned (rotation about -59). One part. Cherry and Madison (20 ft) not used.

sheet-3-1.description: Part 1 of sheet 3 is the main map, covering the area east of the business centre of Washington borough between East Church Street along the top and the Shabecong Creek along the bottom left. East Washington Avenue crosses the middle of the sheet, drawn about 66 ft wide, and North Jackson Avenue and Van Natta cross it from opposite sides with a slight offset, North Jackson Avenue running north to East Church Street and Van Natta and South Jackson Avenue running south. School Street and Hill Street divide the blocks between Church Street and Washington Avenue into narrow residential lots, drawn at 33 ft and 20 ft wide respectively. The district is almost entirely dwellings of frame construction with their barns, sheds and auto garages, with larger lots along East Washington Avenue and open ground at the right, where lot lines are drawn across unbuilt land. The principal building is the First M. E. Church with its attached chapel, which fills the block between Hill Street and North Jackson Avenue south of the Hill Street cross street. A pink-coloured brick works with a long shed stands at the left edge on East Washington Avenue, a watchmaker's shop is lettered on School Street, and a private workshop and storage building stand in the right-hand blocks. The Delaware, Lackawanna and Western Railroad is drawn as a diagonal line at the top right beside the compass rose and the date stamp for June 1924. A temporary note beside Hill Street says that the location of a building was not learned at the time of survey. The lower right of the sheet is a boxed area set off by a heavy line, which is a separate part and is not covered here. The scale is 50 ft to an inch and the sheet is turned about 15 degrees from north. Adjoining sheets are 2, 12, 15 and 17.
notes: East Church is today East Church Street, and East Washington Avenue is East Washington Avenue; Van Natta is today Vannatta Street, and North Jackson Avenue between East Church and East Washington is Jackson Avenue.
Control point East Washington Avenue / Vannatta Street is hand-picked: the detector paired the street's right edge with the heavy box line of the lower right part and placed it 22 ft off.
East Church Street / Hill Street is hand-picked, since Hill Street is only 20 ft wide.
East Church Street / School Street was not used: School Street bends away to the northwest and its modern node lies about 12 percent farther from Hill Street than the drawn junction.
The lower right box (Nassau Road, Jos. Kreidel feed mill, Mill Pond, Tail Race) is part 2 and is not georeferenced.
50 ft. Part 1: E Church, School, Hill, N/S Jackson Av, E Washington Av, Van Natta. Part 2 lower-right box (Nassau Road fork, Jos. Kreidel feed mill) unplaced.

Not georeferenced on this sheet: lower-right box: Nassau Road fork, Jos. Kreidel feed mill, mill pond (no street junction in OSM (Nassau Road not in OSM); needs carried points if sheet 15 or 17 redraw the mill).

sheet-4.description: Sheet 4 shows the northern edge of Washington borough and the adjoining part of Washington Township, an open district of scattered dwellings. The sheet is turned about 32 degrees so that north points toward the upper right, with a compass rose at the right. Belvidere Avenue, a 45 ft street drawn with a water main, runs the length of the sheet from top to bottom just right of centre. Rush Avenue, also lettered North Lincoln, runs parallel to it on the left, and the two are joined by Independent Street and, near the top, by Wyckoff Lane, a 25 ft lane that ends at the edge of Belvidere Avenue. Hatcher's Lane and Green run diagonally to the right from Belvidere Avenue and carry a few narrow lots with dwellings, barns and chicken houses, those on Green with long chicken houses and a garage with a five-car capacity. A dash-dot line from the upper left to Hatcher's Lane is the borough line, lettered Washington on one side and Township on the other. Most of the sheet is open ground divided by property lines and carries only a handful of detached frame dwellings, a greenhouse, sheds and barns. The dry bed of the former Morris Canal curves across the lower left corner. Most blocks are numbered with the lot numbers of the borough. The scale is 50 ft to an inch, and the sheet carries the date stamp for June 1924 and the sheet's scale bar at the lower right. Adjoining sheets are 5 and 6 below it and, on the left, 5 and the margin of the town; the areas left blank belong to other sheets or lie outside the survey.
notes: Independent is today Independence Street, Green is Green Street, and Rush Avenue (N. Lincoln) is Rush Street; Wyckoff Lane appears to be the modern Independent Street, since the modern node lies where the lane meets Belvidere Avenue.
Hatcher's Lane has no modern equivalent in OpenStreetMap.
The fit rests on five points that agree to only about 3 m (leave-one-out about 7.6 m), because the drawn streets turn up to 3 degrees from the modern ones; treat as low confidence.
Belvidere Avenue / Green Street and Rush / Wyckoff Lane are hand-picked.
50 ft. North end: Wyckoff Lane, Rush Av, Independent (= Independence Street), Green, Belvidere Av, Hatcher's Lane. One part; low confidence (drawn streets turned 2-3 degrees from modern).

sheet-5-1.description: The main part of sheet 5 covers the north-west edge of Washington between North Lincoln Avenue and Van Liew Avenue, north of Carlton Avenue, drawn at 50 ft to an inch. It wraps around two separate insets in the upper left of the sheet (Bowerstown and Brass Castle), which are set off by heavy lines. North Lincoln Avenue runs along the east edge of the sheet, with only its west side drawn; Parker Avenue leaves it to the east. Along the west side of North Lincoln Avenue is a row of frame dwellings lettered 'colored dwellings', with the Mount Pisgah A.M.E. Church among them. Carlton Avenue, 52 ft wide with a water pipe, runs along the bottom of the sheet; its north side is lined with two-story frame dwellings numbered 34 to 60, and two 16 ft alleys and a 20 ft alley lead north from it into the deep block behind. At the west end, Van Liew Avenue comes in diagonally to meet Carlton Avenue where Grand Avenue begins to the south. The rest of the area is open land, with farm buildings, sheds, a wagon shed, an ice house and a barn and chicken house on the large lots behind the street fronts. The street grid is turned about 30 degrees on the page, as on the neighbouring sheets.
notes: Parker Avenue is New Street today; Van Liew Avenue is not in the modern street data under that name.
Mount Pisgah A.M.E. Church on North Lincoln Avenue.

sheet-6.description: Sheet 6 covers the north end of Washington borough between North Lincoln Avenue at the left edge and the dry bed of the Morris Canal at the right, from Carlton Avenue at the bottom to open ground at the top. The sheet is turned about 31 degrees, with north toward the upper right. Parker Avenue, also lettered Park Avenue, and Carlton Avenue cross the sheet from left to right, joined by Cherry Street, a 20 ft street, and by Belvidere Avenue, drawn 50 ft wide, which narrows and bends where it meets the canal bed. Between Parker Avenue and Carlton Avenue the blocks hold a row of detached frame dwellings on narrow lots along Belvidere Avenue, with chicken houses, barns and a few dwellings on the larger lots to the west. North of Parker Avenue the left half of the sheet is open ground with an ice house, a log pile with a traction engine and saw, and scattered chicken houses. The dry bed of the former Morris Canal and its tow path cross the sheet diagonally from the upper left to the lower right; east of Belvidere Avenue it carries a railroad on a trestle with an inclined track, coal pockets, a chute and a coal and lumber yard with warehouses, lumber sheds and a lumber warehouse, reached from Cleveland Street. At the upper right the Standard Oil Co. depot has oil tanks, a pump house, a warehouse and a tank car siding. Water mains are lettered along the main streets, with hydrants at the corners. The scale is 50 ft to an inch, and the sheet bears the date stamp for June 1924, a compass rose and a scale bar. Adjoining sheets are 4 above, 8 and 9 below and 5 to the left.
notes: Parker Avenue (Park Avenue) is today New Street; Cherry Street north of Carlton Avenue is Cherry Street and, up to New Street, Lee Court.

Cherry Street is drawn 20 ft wide, and the detector put its junctions 35 ft off by pairing a lot line; Carlton Avenue / Cherry Street is hand-picked, and the Lee Court / New Street node, 4.9 m off the fit, was left out.
The canal and tow path are lettered 'Dry bed of former Morris Canal'; the coal and lumber works carry the name Catelle (read at medium confidence).

sheet-7.description: Sheet 7 shows a residential district of Washington borough west of North Lincoln Avenue, bounded by Carlton Avenue along the top, Grand Avenue on the left and North Lincoln Avenue on the right. The sheet is turned about 22 degrees, with north pointing toward the upper left and a compass rose at the top left corner. Carlton Avenue, drawn about 45 ft wide, runs across the top and continues to the left as Van Liew Avenue, which bends at the sheet edge. West Warren Street and West Johnston Avenue run from Grand Avenue to North Lincoln Avenue and divide the sheet into three tiers of blocks. Between Carlton Avenue and West Warren a 16 ft side lane curves off a narrow back street, and a 10 ft lane runs between West Warren and West Johnston Avenue. The buildings are almost all detached frame dwellings of one and two stories with barns, sheds and poultry houses on deep lots; the houses are densest along Carlton Avenue and West Johnston Avenue near North Lincoln Avenue, and Grand Avenue has larger vacant parcels with poultry houses. Two larger buildings stand out: an auto painting shop with a capacity of 20 cars on the north side of West Johnston Avenue, drawn in blue for a masonry building with a concrete floor, and the First Baptist Church at the corner of North Lincoln Avenue, heated by steam and lit by electricity and gas. Water mains of 4, 6 and 10 inches are lettered along all streets, with hydrants at the corners. The sheet is drawn at 50 ft to an inch and carries the June 1924 date stamp and a scale bar. Adjoining sheets are 5 above, 8 and 11 to the right, 10 below, and 16 and 55 to the left.
notes: West Johnston Avenue is today West Johnston Street and West Warren is West Warren Street. Van Liew Avenue has no equivalent in OpenStreetMap.

North Lincoln Avenue / West Johnston Street was not detected; a hand-picked point agreed with the other five only to 3.5 m, so West Johnston Street may lie a few metres off its old line and the point was left out.
The sheet shows the First Baptist Church (read as 1st Baptist Church) on West Johnston Avenue at North Lincoln Avenue.
50 ft. Carlton Av, W Warren, W Johnston Av, Grand Av, Van Liew Av, N Lincoln Av. One part.

sheet-8.description: Sheet 8 shows a regular grid of residential blocks in the north part of Washington borough, from Carlton Avenue at the top to East and West Johnston Avenue at the bottom and from North Lincoln Avenue at the left to Cleveland Street at the right. The sheet is turned about 31 degrees, with north pointing toward the upper right and a compass rose on the right edge. Cherry Street, a 20 ft street, and Belvidere Avenue, 50 ft wide, run down the sheet and are crossed by West Warren and East Warren, which change name at Belvidere Avenue, and by West Johnston Avenue and East Johnston Avenue. Most blocks hold detached frame dwellings of two or two and a half stories on deep lots with barns, sheds and poultry houses behind them; a row of six dwellings of the same plan stands on North Lincoln Avenue at West Warren. Non-residential buildings are few: an auto sales building with a capacity of 15 cars and a large building lettered Cobbles, both drawn in blue for concrete or cement-block construction, with two brick buildings behind, on Carlton Avenue at Belvidere Avenue; St. Joseph's R.C. Church, heated by hot air furnace and lit by electricity, on Belvidere Avenue between East Warren and Cherry Street; and a garage and tire shop for six cars at the top right. Three blocks at the lower left carry a row of chicken houses and an incubator. Water mains and hydrants are lettered along the streets. The scale is 50 ft to an inch and the sheet carries the June 1924 date stamp and a scale bar. Adjoining sheets are 6 above, 7 to the left, 9 and 17 to the right and 11 below.
notes: West and East Warren are today West Warren Street and East Warren Street; West and East Johnston Avenue are West Johnston Street and East Johnston Street.
Cherry Street is only 20 ft wide and its junctions were not used as control points; North Lincoln Avenue / West Johnston Street was not detected.
50 ft. Carlton Av to Johnston Av, N Lincoln Av to Cleveland. One part.

sheet-9-1.description: The main part of sheet 9 covers the north-east edge of Washington between Cleveland Street and the Delaware, Lackawanna and Western Railroad, from the canal north of East Warren down to East Johnson Avenue, drawn at 50 ft to an inch. Cleveland and Taylor run north to south and are crossed by East Warren and East Johnson Avenue; the blocks between them (17 and 18) are thinly built, with frame dwellings facing Taylor and Cleveland and much open ground behind. East of Taylor the D. L. & W. R. R. tracks, with sidings and an iron bridge, run diagonally across the sheet beside the dry bed of the former Morris Canal and its tow path. North of East Warren, between the canal tow path and the tracks, stands the Burwood Corporation, a factory of steel skeleton and concrete with brick curtain walls making moving picture machines (assembling only), on old canal foundations. At the corner of Taylor and East Johnson Avenue stands the New Jersey Power & Light Co. power house and company garage, the power house noted as not in use. Water pipes run in East Warren, Taylor and East Johnson Avenue. Heavy lines set off two separate parts in the upper right of the sheet, both on Morris Turnpike west of the town: a sewage disposal works at 100 ft to an inch and the N.J. Interurban Co. car barn 3 1/2 miles west of the post office; they are not part of this area.
notes: East Johnson Avenue is printed so; it is East Johnston Street today. East Warren is East Warren Street.
Burwood Corporation, manufacturers of moving picture machines, beside the canal bed.
New Jersey Power & Light Co. power house (not in use) and company garage at Taylor and East Johnson Avenue.
The Morris Canal is drawn as a dry bed with its tow path.

Three parts: 1 main (Cleveland St, Taylor, E Warren, E Johnson Av, D.L.&W. R.R., Morris Canal bed, Burwood Corp.), configured by the lead; 2 inset at 100 ft on Morris Turnpike (sewage disposal beds) and 3 inset 3.5 miles W of P.O. (N.J. Interurban car barn) left unplaced.

Not georeferenced on this sheet: inset at 100 ft: Morris Turnpike west of the borough line, sewage disposal filtering beds, house numbers 401-413 (no street junction (only a 15 ft lane to the brook); needs hand-picked control on West Washington Avenue about 200 to 400 m west of the borough line).

Not georeferenced on this sheet: inset: N.J. Interurban Co. sub-power station and car barn on Morris Turnpike, 3 1/2 miles west of the post office (no street junction; only Morris Turnpike drawn; needs the site of the car barn on NJ 57 west of Washington).

sheet-10.description: Sheet 10 covers the western residential blocks of Washington borough, between West Stewart Street at the top and West Washington Avenue at the bottom, with North Lincoln Avenue running diagonally down the right side of the page. State Street crosses the middle of the sheet and West Church Street joins Lincoln Avenue at the lower right. North Wandling Avenue runs north to south through the centre between Stewart and Washington; south of Washington Avenue the street continues as South Wandling Avenue, drawn offset to the west. A 20 ft alley, unnamed on the sheet, runs east and west between Stewart and State streets. The area is almost entirely dwellings: detached frame houses of one and a half to two and a half stories with porches, with stables, sheds and auto garages behind them, on deep lots; the densest row, between State Street and West Washington Avenue, faces Washington Avenue with house numbers in the 100s. A few buildings are coloured pink (brick), one near the foot of North Wandling Avenue. Several large blocks in the upper left carry only a few houses and are otherwise open lots. Water pipes of 4 and 6 inches are marked along Stewart, State and Wandling, with fire hydrants at corners. Block and lot numbers are printed along the street lines. The sheet is drawn at 50 ft to an inch and carries a north arrow on the right, with the grid turned from the page. Adjoining sheets are 7 above, 11 to the east, 16 to the west, 13 below and 2 at the lower right.
notes: West Stewart, State, West Church, West Washington Avenue, North and South Wandling Avenue and North Lincoln Avenue are West Stewart Street, State Street, West Church Street, West Washington Avenue, North and South Wandling Avenue and North Lincoln Avenue today.
North and South Wandling Avenue are drawn offset across West Washington Avenue; the control uses the south street at its junction with Washington Avenue.
An unlabelled 20 ft alley between Stewart and State streets was not used for control.
50 ft. W Stewart, State, W Church, W Washington Av, N/S Wandling Av, N Lincoln Av. One part.

sheet-11.description: Sheet 11 covers four blocks in the centre of Washington, north of the business district, bounded by West and East Johnston Avenue on the north, North Lincoln Avenue on the west, West and East Church Street on the south and Taylor Street on the east. Belvidere Avenue runs north to south through the middle of the sheet and divides the West and East halves of the cross streets; West and East Stewart Street cross it with a short offset. The blocks west of Belvidere Avenue are cut by two narrow side streets, Madison Street and Cherry Street, both drawn about 20 ft wide. The area is almost entirely residential: detached frame dwellings of one and a half to two and a half stories with porches, stables, sheds and auto garages behind them, set on deep lots. Larger houses face Belvidere Avenue and East Johnston Avenue. At the south end of the east side, facing East Church Street near Belvidere Avenue, stands the Hotel Windsor, a large frame building with its outbuildings, and a doctor's office stands on the block between East Stewart and East Church streets. Cleveland Street runs north from East Stewart to East Johnston Avenue. Water pipes are marked along Johnston, Stewart, Church and Belvidere, with fire hydrants at several corners. The sheet is drawn at 50 ft to an inch and turned so that the street grid runs square to the page; north points to the upper left. Adjoining sheets are 7, 8, 9, 10, 12 and 2.
notes: Johnston Avenue is today West and East Johnston Street; Stewart and Church are West and East Stewart Street and West and East Church Street.
Hotel Windsor on East Church Street at Belvidere Avenue.
Madison Street and Cherry Street are drawn about 20 ft wide and were left out of the control points.
50 ft. W/E Johnston Av, W/E Stewart, W/E Church, N Lincoln Av, Madison, Cherry, Belvidere Av, Cleveland, Taylor. One part. Pilot. Madison and Cherry (20 ft) left out of control.

sheet-12.description: Sheet 12 covers the east side of Washington borough, from East Johnston Avenue at the top to East Church Street at the bottom, between Taylor Street on the west and North Jackson Avenue on the east. The drawing is turned so that the streets run at an angle to the page. A broad diagonal belt of railroad tracks (the D.L. & W. R. R.) crosses the sheet from the upper centre to the lower right, with a road running beside it, and the dry bed of the former Morris Canal and its tow path cross the top. West of the tracks, School Street runs diagonally from East Stewart Street to East Church Street. Along East Stewart Street and Hahn Street are rows of frame dwellings, and at the top the Washington Coal and Supply Company yard, with coal pockets, wagon shed and firewood sheds, lies beside the tracks. On the west side of School Street are the Washington Public School, a large brick building with an auditorium, stage and scenery room, and, on Taylor Street, a chapel and the First Presbyterian Church, both coloured pink for brick. South of Hahn Street the Florey Bros. piano manufactory, with assembling and finishing, a cabinet shop and powered, steam-heated buildings, fronts Florey Street, which is also lettered Brown Street. Narrow lots run down to East Church Street, lined with dwellings. East of the tracks, North Jackson Avenue is built up on its west side with houses, and the area to its east is largely open, with Gibson Place and Jackson Plaza lettered as lanes. The sheet is drawn at 50 ft to an inch with a north arrow at the lower left. Sheet numbers 9, 11, 2, 3 and 16 are lettered at the margins for the adjoining sheets.
notes: East Johnston Avenue, East Stewart, East Church and North Jackson Avenue are East Johnston Street, East Stewart Street, East Church Street and Jackson Avenue today; Florey Street (Brown Street) is Brown Street.

Modern East Stewart Street and Hahn Street run on past the drawn ends of the streets near the railroad, and some modern junctions here (Stewart and Taylor, Brown and School) did not match the drawn ones; they were left out of the control.
The part has only four control points and is low confidence.
50 ft. E Johnston, E Stewart, Hahn, Florey (Brown) St, E Church, Taylor, School, N Jackson Av, railroad; Washington Public School, Florey Bros piano works. One part, low confidence (4 points).

sheet-13-1.description: Part 1 of sheet 13 is the upper two thirds of the page, above the heavy line that separates the Washington Porcelain Company box. It shows the south-western edge of Washington borough, between West Washington Avenue along the top and Shabecong Creek along the bottom. South Lincoln Avenue runs diagonally down the right side, and Cornish Street crosses from the left to meet it. South Wandling Avenue, a 20 ft street, runs down the left edge past Cornish, Ophelia (Marble) and Mechanic streets, which are also drawn about 20 ft wide; North Wandling Avenue is lettered north of Washington Avenue, offset from the south street. The area is residential: rows of frame dwellings face West Washington Avenue and South Lincoln Avenue, a row of attached houses stands on the east side of Lincoln Avenue near Cornish Street, and the blocks between Cornish Street and Mechanic Street carry only scattered houses, barns and sheds on large lots. Water pipes of 4 and 6 inches run along Washington Avenue, South Wandling Avenue and Lincoln Avenue. Shabecong Creek crosses the lower part from left to right, with a bridge where South Lincoln Avenue crosses it. The heavy line below the creek steps up near the middle of the page and carries the words No Exposure along it. The right side of the part is blank except for a north arrow and the sheet-number stamp, since that ground belongs to sheet 2. The part is drawn at 50 ft to an inch and turned about 15 degrees. Adjoining sheets are 10 above, 16 to the left, 2 to the right and 14 and the lower box of this sheet below.
notes: West Washington Avenue, Cornish Street, South Lincoln Avenue, South and North Wandling Avenue, Ophelia Street, Marble Street and Mechanic Street keep their names today; Ophelia Street is lettered with Marble in brackets.
South Wandling Avenue is drawn about 600 px (75 ft) west of North Wandling Avenue across West Washington Avenue; control uses the south street.
Cornish, Ophelia, Marble and Mechanic streets and South Wandling Avenue are 20 ft wide and were placed by hand-picked points, not detected.
Low to medium confidence: the control is five points along South Wandling Avenue and two on South Lincoln Avenue.

50 ft. Part 1: W Washington Av, Cornish, Ophelia (Marble), Mechanic, S Wandling, S Lincoln Av (20 ft streets hand-picked). Part 2 box below heavy line (Washington Porcelain Co, Cochran Bros, John Sommer Faucet Co) unplaced.

Not georeferenced on this sheet: box below the heavy line: Washington Porcelain Co., Cochran Bros. brass foundry, John Sommer Faucet Co., Willow (no usable junction; needs carried points from sheet 14 (step 6b)).

sheet-14.description: Sheet 14 covers the southern edge of Washington borough, from Shabecong Creek across the top to the D.L. & W. railroad across the bottom, between a blank western side that belongs to sheet 13 and Broad Street down the right edge. South Lincoln Avenue runs diagonally from the creek at the top, where a bridge carries it across, to the lower centre. Willow Street crosses it east to west about two thirds of the way down, and Monroe Street, a narrow street, joins Lincoln Avenue and Broad Street in the upper right. Youmans Avenue is lettered beside Broad Street at the right edge. Most of the sheet east of Lincoln Avenue is built up with frame dwellings on long narrow lots running back from Broad Street and Lincoln Avenue, and St. Peter's Episcopal Church stands near the right edge, with a garage, monument works and the Washington Knob Company's wooden piano and desk knob factory near the creek. In the lower left are the B. O. Tilden Manufacturing Company's plumbers' wood work plant, with its dry kilns, lumber sheds and transfer tracks, and a celluloid sheet coating works coloured pink. The Washington Gas Company's works with its gas holder, and a former beer depot used partly for ice storage, stand near the railroad. A freight siding runs along the bottom. The sheet is drawn at 50 ft to an inch with a north arrow at the upper left. Adjoining sheets are 13 to the upper left, 2 above, 3 and 15 to the right and 16 below.
notes: South Lincoln Avenue, Willow, Monroe Street, Broad and Youmans Avenue are South Lincoln Avenue, Willow Street, Monroe Street, Broad Street and Youmans Avenue today.
Monroe Street is only about 20 ft wide on the sheet; the detector paired its lower edge with a lot line, so the two Monroe junctions were hand-picked.
Only three control points were available (Monroe and Lincoln, Monroe and Broad, Lincoln and Willow); the part is low confidence.
50 ft. S Lincoln Av, Broad, Willow, Monroe (20 ft, hand-picked), Shabecong Creek, railroad. One part; three-point exact fit, low confidence.

sheet-15-1.description: The main part of sheet 15 covers the south side of Washington east of Broad, from Alleger at the top of the sheet to Youmans Avenue and the edge of the borough park, drawn at 50 ft to an inch. Broad runs down the west edge of the sheet with a continuous row of two-story frame dwellings, numbered 36 to 146, on its east side. Shabecong Creek crosses the sheet from west to east below Alleger; at Broad it passes under a stone and concrete bridge, and next to it on the south bank stands the Washington Steam Laundry, with steam power and heat and electric light. A short Driveway and Drive lead in from Broad on either side of the creek, and a lumber shed stands on the north bank. Youmans Avenue, 48 ft wide with a water pipe, runs east from Broad to Van Natta and is lined on both sides with two-story frame dwellings. A Park Entrance, about 55 ft wide, leads south from Youmans Avenue into the borough park, and a second Park Entrance, 20 ft wide, leads east from Broad near the bottom of the sheet; the park itself is not drawn ('no exposure, park beyond'). The lower right of the sheet, beyond a heavy line, is a separate part showing Morris Turnpike at the road to Asbury, west of the borough.
notes: Van Natta is Vannatta Street today; the Park Entrance off Youmans Avenue is Lower Park Road.
The Park Entrance off Broad near the bottom of the sheet lies about 30 m north of where Upper Park Drive meets Broad today, so it was not used as a control point.
Washington Steam Laundry on Broad at Shabecong Creek.
Placed from four points: one detected (Van Natta / Youmans Avenue) and three hand-picked along Broad and at the Park Entrance.

50 ft. Two parts: 1 main (Broad, Alleger, Youmans Av, Van Natta, Park Entrance = Lower Park Road); 2 lower box on Morris Turnpike (W Washington Av) at the Road to Asbury (Mill Pond Road), 2.4 km west, anchored on one hand-picked point. Configured by the lead.

sheet-15-2.description: The lower right part of sheet 15, set off by a heavy line, shows a short stretch of Morris Turnpike where the Road to Asbury leaves it to the south, west of Washington on the way to Brass Castle, drawn at 50 ft to an inch. Only the south side of the turnpike is drawn; the north side is marked vacant opposite. The Road to Asbury is about 30 ft wide and runs south past farm land (lots 127 and 128) to a farm shed near the bottom of the sheet. At the corner stand frame dwellings and the shops of S. Lanning & Son, auto tops and painting, with a paint shop of solid concrete, sheds and chicken houses. East of the road a brook flows south under the turnpike, which crosses it on a culvert. The part has its own north arrow, turned about 20 to 25 degrees clockwise from the page, and shares the sheet's scale of 50 ft to an inch.
notes: Morris Turnpike is West Washington Avenue (NJ 57) today; the Road to Asbury is Mill Pond Road.
S. Lanning & Son, auto tops and painting.
Placed from one hand-picked point (Mill Pond Road / West Washington Avenue) with the atlas scale and north at 25 degrees, taken from the bearing of the modern turnpike; low confidence.

50 ft. Two parts: 1 main (Broad, Alleger, Youmans Av, Van Natta, Park Entrance = Lower Park Road); 2 lower box on Morris Turnpike (W Washington Av) at the Road to Asbury (Mill Pond Road), 2.4 km west, anchored on one hand-picked point. Configured by the lead.

sheet-16-1.description: The main part of sheet 16 covers the west side of Washington along West Washington Avenue, drawn at 100 ft to an inch. Grand Avenue runs north from West Washington Avenue past State, North Stewart and West Johnson Avenue to West Warren, with dwellings on its east side; the blocks west of it toward the sheet's dividing line are largely open lots. Along West Washington Avenue the frontage is lined with frame dwellings, many of them numbered, from Prospect Street east to South Wandling Avenue. At the west end, between lettered lots, stands Eckel's Washington Filling Station with its gasoline storage tanks, and east of it a public garage of hollow tile with steel girders. Gardner Court is a short row of attached dwellings running south from West Washington Avenue next to Prospect Street, and a proposed street is marked off Prospect Street. In the south-east corner the sheet shows Cornish Street, Marble, Ophelia Street and Mechanic Street meeting South Wandling Avenue, with a garage of concrete block and a solid concrete chicken house. Much of the area south of West Washington Avenue (lots 2 and 137) is left blank. Water pipes are marked along West Washington Avenue, Grand Avenue and South Wandling Avenue. The upper left of the sheet, beyond a heavy line, is a separate part showing South Lincoln Avenue and Broad Street south of the borough line. North points straight up the page.
notes: West Johnson Avenue is printed so; it is West Johnston Street today. North Stewart is West Stewart Street.
Eckel's Washington Filling Station on West Washington Avenue.
Of the two modern nodes where Grand Avenue meets West Stewart Street, 34 m apart, the sheet draws only the northern one; the southern was excluded.

100 ft to an inch. Two parts: 1 main (W Washington Av, Grand Av, State, N. Stewart, W. Johnson Av, Prospect, Cornish, Wandling); 2 upper left box south of the borough (S Lincoln Av, Broad, Nunn Av, Mozart Av, County Road = Washburn Avenue). Configured by the lead.

sheet-16-2.description: The upper left part of sheet 16, set off by a heavy line, shows the south end of Washington where South Lincoln Avenue and Broad converge toward the borough line, drawn at 100 ft to an inch. Nunn Avenue comes in from the west to South Lincoln Avenue, Mozart Avenue runs east from Broad, and County Road crosses both South Lincoln Avenue and Broad near the bottom of the part. The borough line, drawn as a dash-dot line, cuts diagonally across the lower part, and the land south of it is lettered Washington Township. Development is thin: frame dwellings of one and two stories with sheds and outbuildings line Broad and South Lincoln Avenue, and a two-story garage of concrete block for eight cars, with steam heat and electric lights, stands at the corner of Broad and Mozart Avenue. The Washington Township Hall stands at the south end of Broad below County Road. Water pipes are marked in South Lincoln Avenue and Broad. Lot numbers 3, 26, 26 1/3, 144 and 146 refer to the key map. The railroad crosses the very top of the part. The part is drawn at a slightly different angle from the main part of the sheet.
notes: County Road is today Washburn Avenue.
Washington Township Hall on Broad south of County Road.
Placed from four points: two detected (Broad / Mozart, Nunn / South Lincoln) and two hand-picked on County Road; scale 3.97 px/ft against about 4.04 for the atlas.

100 ft to an inch. Two parts: 1 main (W Washington Av, Grand Av, State, N. Stewart, W. Johnson Av, Prospect, Cornish, Wandling); 2 upper left box south of the borough (S Lincoln Av, Broad, Nunn Av, Mozart Av, County Road = Washburn Avenue). Configured by the lead.

sheet-17-1.description: Part 1 of sheet 17 is the main map on the lower and right-hand part of the page, drawn at 100 ft to an inch, below and to the left of the heavy lines that enclose two 50 ft enlargements at the top. It covers the east side of Washington borough along the creek and the railroad. East Washington Avenue crosses the upper left, lined with frame dwellings, and Shabecong Creek runs from the lower left to the upper right across the middle. North and South Jackson Avenue and Van Natta meet East Washington Avenue at the left edge. A broad diagonal belt of D.L. & W. railroad tracks and Railroad Avenue runs from East Washington Avenue to the lower right, with the Phillipsburg Branch crossing the bottom. On the north side of Railroad Avenue the ground is mostly open; the Washington Silk Mills of Louis Roessel and Company stand beside the creek and Railroad Avenue, and a note refers the reader to the enlarged plan above. In the left half, Youmans Avenue and Park Avenue run across the page past rows of frame dwellings, including a pink brick row on Youmans Avenue, and the Pohatcong Hosiery Mills Inc. plant at the lower left carries the same reference to its enlarged plan. A new grid of Youmans, Beethoven and Fisher avenues is laid out between Railroad Avenue and the railroad at the lower right, with scattered houses, and O'Shea Alley runs along the bottom edge. The part is turned about 16 degrees from the page. Sheet numbers 3, 15 and 22 are lettered at the margins for adjoining sheets.
notes: East Washington Avenue, North Jackson Avenue, Youmans Avenue, Park Avenue, Railroad Avenue, Beethoven Avenue and Fisher Avenue keep their names today; Van Natta is Vannatta Street and O'Shea Alley is Oshea Street.
Scale is 100 ft to an inch, as lettered on the sheet; the fitted scale is 4.01 px/ft.
The modern Vannatta and Youmans junction did not match the drawn one and was left out of the control; five control points are in use.

100 ft main. Part 1 main (E Washington Av, Jackson Av, Park Av, Railroad Av, Fisher Av, D.L.&W. depot); part 2 upper-left box at 50 ft (Washington Silk Mills), carried from part 1; part 3 upper-right box at 50 ft (Pohatcong), anchored on NJ 31 / Park Avenue.

sheet-17-2.description: Part 2 of sheet 17 is the box at the upper left of the page, an enlarged plan drawn at 50 ft to an inch of the Washington Silk Mills of Louis Roessel and Company, whose location is marked on the main map below. Shabecong Creek crosses the upper left corner. The mill is a long pink brick building with a smaller pink brick power or boiler house beside it; the notes lettered here describe night watchman, electric lights, sprinklers, wet system connected to borough mains, and a pressure tank, and mark the structures with automatic sprinkler circles. A yellow frame storage building lies to the south, lettered not to belong to the Washington Silk Mills, and another small frame building stands near the centre. Railroad Avenue runs diagonally across the right half from upper left to lower right, with 8 inch water pipe along it, a fire hydrant, and a north arrow beside it. The heavy lines on the right and the bottom mark the limits of the box. The part has no complete street junction and was placed from two corners of the mill building carried from the main map.
notes: Placed from two mill building corners carried from part 1 and the configured scale; low confidence.
Railroad Avenue is still named Railroad Avenue.

100 ft main. Part 1 main (E Washington Av, Jackson Av, Park Av, Railroad Av, Fisher Av, D.L.&W. depot); part 2 upper-left box at 50 ft (Washington Silk Mills), carried from part 1; part 3 upper-right box at 50 ft (Pohatcong), anchored on NJ 31 / Park Avenue.

sheet-17-3.description: Part 3 of sheet 17 is the box at the upper right of the page, an enlarged plan drawn at 50 ft to an inch of the Pohatcong Hosiery Mills Inc., whose location is marked on the main map. Park Avenue runs across the top from Van Natta, a narrow street on the left edge lettered Park Opposite, and the rest of the box is taken up by the mill plant. The Old Mill, a long narrow pink brick building lettered Manufacturing, runs north and south, with the New Mill (manufacturing and shipping) to its east, joined by concrete and iron bridges, and a laboratory and office, a drug room, fire house and pump house with a tower close by. Notes describe a night watchman with clock, power and lights by electricity and heat by steam, hose, buckets and extinguishers, iron posts and girders and wood posts and floor beams. A coal shed and storage of chemicals stand at the foot. Further south the box is empty except for the faint outline of the railroad tracks across the lower right. Water pipes of 4 and 6 inches and hydrants are marked on the streets. The heavy lines on the left and at the bottom divide the box from the other parts of the sheet. The part is placed from one junction, Van Natta and Park Avenue, and a derived second point, so it is low confidence.
notes: Van Natta is NJ 31 / Vannatta Street in the modern data; Park Avenue keeps its name.
Anchored on one hand-picked junction (NJ 31 and Park Avenue) with the configured scale and north; low confidence.

100 ft main. Part 1 main (E Washington Av, Jackson Av, Park Av, Railroad Av, Fisher Av, D.L.&W. depot); part 2 upper-left box at 50 ft (Washington Silk Mills), carried from part 1; part 3 upper-right box at 50 ft (Pohatcong), anchored on NJ 31 / Park Avenue.

sheet-18-1.description: Part 1 of sheet 18 is the main map, drawn at 100 ft to an inch, covering the lower two thirds of the page and the strip along its right side, below the Gibson Park box and the Myrtle Avenue strip at the top. East Washington Avenue runs across the bottom of the page, and Shabecong Creek crosses the whole part from the lower left, under a bridge at Prosper Way, to the upper right, with a second bridge where the lane called Bryan Avenue crosses it. The upper left is the Gibson Park subdivision, a laid-out but largely unbuilt tract of numbered blocks with Prosper Way, a 70 ft street along the left edge, and Mc Kinley Avenue curving beside a grove, with Gibson Place, Harrison, Jefferson Avenue, a foot path and Washington Plaza at the south end by the creek. Only a few houses stand on the blocks along East Washington Avenue, and the central and right-hand ground is almost empty. Along the creek at the lower centre stand the Victory Silk Company and, at the right, the greenhouses of Alonzo J. Bryan, with packing, propagating and work buildings, a private water supply of 500,000 gallons and a reservoir noted at an elevation of 168 ft. A dash-dot line near the right edge marks the borough boundary, and a compass rose stands near the middle. Blocks 165, 170 to 172, 175 and 176 and the numbers 16 and 177 are lettered, and the scale of 100 ft to an inch is lettered at the foot.
notes: Prosper Way and East Washington Avenue keep their names today; Jefferson Avenue is Jefferson Street and Mc Kinley Avenue is McKinley Avenue. Harrison and Bryan Avenue have no counterpart in the modern data near here.
Gibson Park was laid out but not built as drawn; modern Van Buren Street, Gibson Place and McKinley Avenue junctions disagreed with the drawn blocks by 4 to 6 m and were left out of the control.
Placed from two points on Prosper Way (Jefferson Street and East Washington Avenue) with the configured scale; the east end along East Washington Avenue may be tens of metres off. Low confidence.
100 ft. Part 1 main (E Washington Av, Prosper Way, Jefferson Av, Gibson Park), anchored; part 2 Myrtle Avenue strip unplaced; part 3 Gibson Park box, anchored.
Not georeferenced on this sheet: Myrtle Avenue strip (no junction; Myrtle meets modern streets about 300 m west of the sheet; needs hand-picked or parcel-corner control).

sheet-18-3.description: Part 3 of sheet 18 is the box at the upper left of the page, bounded by heavy lines on all sides, which draws the part of the Gibson Park tract lying west of Prosper Way. Prosper Way, a 70 ft street, runs north and south down the right side of the box. Harrison runs east and west along the top of the box, a 30 ft street, and Jefferson Avenue curves in from the lower left to meet Prosper Way a little below the middle, also drawn 30 ft wide. Garfield is lettered on a short street at the upper left. The area is subdivided into narrow lots in blocks 174 and 176, with a few small buildings, most of them in the block north of Jefferson Avenue and two coloured blue near the foot of block 176. Washington Plaza is lettered at the south end, where Shabecong Creek enters from the left, passes under a bridge at Prosper Way and leaves the box at the right. A fan of narrow lots runs along the diagonal heavy line at the left. The box is drawn at about 100 ft to an inch and carries its own north arrow at the lower left. The ground to the right of Prosper Way is blank and belongs to the main map. The part has only one junction, Jefferson and Prosper Way, so it is placed from it with a configured scale, and it is low confidence.
notes: Jefferson Avenue is Jefferson Street today; Harrison and Garfield have no counterpart in the modern data here.
Anchored on the Jefferson and Prosper Way junction with the configured scale; low confidence.
100 ft. Part 1 main (E Washington Av, Prosper Way, Jefferson Av, Gibson Park), anchored; part 2 Myrtle Avenue strip unplaced; part 3 Gibson Park box, anchored.
Not georeferenced on this sheet: Myrtle Avenue strip (no junction; Myrtle meets modern streets about 300 m west of the sheet; needs hand-picked or parcel-corner control).

sheet-19-1.description: Most of sheet 19 shows Port Colden, an unincorporated village of about 300 people in Washington Township, drawn at 100 ft to an inch. Church Street runs south from the top of the sheet past a Methodist Episcopal church, the public school and a few dozen frame dwellings, and Basin Street branches east from it beside the school. The street is lettered Church in the upper half and Front in the lower half, and reaches the Morris Turnpike at the foot of the sheet, where the Road to Changewater leaves it to the south. Lock Street runs parallel to Front Street on the west, lined with small lots and dwellings numbered 200 to 221, with a drive and a wagon house at its head. West of Lock Street the sheet is mostly open farm land; the compass rose stands in this blank area. The diagonal bed of the former Morris Canal crosses the sheet from the upper left to the junction, with a former canal basin and a tow path east of Front Street. At the bottom the Morris Turnpike runs across the sheet with a row of dwellings along its north side, and the D.L.&W. railroad and County Road run diagonally below it. The lower right corner carries the scale bar and the Princeton map-division stamp. The upper left of the sheet is a separate box, with the Washington-Port Colden Road and the N.J. Interurban Co. property, which is not included in this part.
notes: Front Street and Church Street are today Port Colden Road; the Morris Turnpike is NJ 57 (West Washington Avenue and East Washington Avenue); County Road is Washburn Avenue.

Placed from one hand-picked point, the junction of the Morris Turnpike with Front Street (NJ 57 / Port Colden Road), with scale 4.04 px/ft taken from the 100 ft scale bar and north at 8 degrees from the sheet's north arrow and the bearing of Port Colden Road; low confidence. Modern Lock Street joins Port Colden Road north of the turnpike, not at it as drawn.
The modern line of NJ 57 west of Front Street is bent away from the straight turnpike drawn here (up to about 100 ft).
100 ft. Port Colden. Part 1 main (Church, Front = Port Colden Road, Basin, Lock, Morris Turnpike), anchored on one hand-picked point; parts 2 (top box) and 3 (car barn box) unplaced.
Not georeferenced on this sheet: top box: Washington-Port Colden Road and turnpike strip (no junction; needs parcel corners (step 6b)).
Not georeferenced on this sheet: lower box: N.J. Interurban Co. car barn, about 1000 ft from Front St (no junction; needs parcel corners (step 6b)).

sheet-20-3.description: The western part of sheet 20 shows Port Murray on the west side of the D.L.&W. railroad, drawn at 50 ft to an inch. A heavy line along the railroad separates it from the village east of the tracks. Main Street runs down the sheet on the west side, a street about 33 to 50 ft wide lined on its west side with numbered lots (about 107 to 190) and frame dwellings, and bends south-east at the lower end to reach the steel and concrete bridge over the railroad. Anderson Lane, a narrow lane of about 20 ft, leaves Main Street to the west, and Canal Street, a street about 40 ft wide, does the same lower down, running past a barn and a few dwellings towards the dry bed of the former Morris Canal at the left edge. In the upper part a public school stands inside the wedge where the heavy line turns, and an unnamed road crosses from Main Street to the railroad. The railroad yard fills the right side of the part, with the freight and passenger depot, a platform, the Port Murray Dairy Co. with its shipping platform and ice house, a water tank and a coal pocket, beside a driveway that runs south-west beyond the bridge. A compass rose stands in the open ground below Anderson Lane, with a note about scattered logs. The upper left corner of the sheet is a separate box showing a farm west of the station.
notes: Main Street is still Main Street; Anderson Lane is the Hoffman Road side of the junction. Canal Street's modern counterpart is uncertain (Canal Lane is not drawn the same way).

sheet-21-1.description: Most of sheet 21 shows Changewater, an unincorporated village of about 200 people on the Musconetcong River, drawn at 100 ft to an inch. At the head of the sheet Fox Lane runs south-west across the upper left past a few dwellings and meets Main Street; the D.L.&W.R.R. passenger station and a milk station of J.J. Bower Co. of Paterson stand at the upper right. Main Street runs south-east towards the Hopatcong Worsted Mills. The mills stand where the D.L.&W. railroad (the Hampton Branch) crosses the tail race and the river, with the mill pond, head race and wool storage around them; an enlarged plan of the mills is given in the inset at the lower left. The Road to Hampton curves along the river's north-west bank and joins County Road, which runs south past the Changewater M.E. Church to a three-way junction. There the Road to Port Murray (also called County Road) runs east-south-east past dwellings numbered 101 to 112 to Dairy Run Road and a stream at the right edge, and another road goes south-west. The Musconetcong River crosses the sheet from the left edge, loops round the mills and leaves at the right. At the top left a group of crude oil storage tanks of the Tidewater Oil Co. is noted, about 400 ft away. A compass rose stands at the left; 'Steep Wooded Hillside' is lettered along the left margin.
notes: The sheet is turned: north points to the left (about 106 degrees counterclockwise from straight up, from the compass rose).

sheet-21-2.description: The inset at the lower left of sheet 21 shows the Hopatcong Worsted Mills at Changewater at 50 ft to an inch, twice the scale of the rest of the sheet, set off by a heavy border. The mill is a large manufacturing building of brick and frame with a manufacturing and office wing at its west end and a one-storey manufacturing addition at its east end, drawn with its sprinkler and hose data (a 3,000 gallon elevated tank filled by a small pump, hose as shown, night watchman with clock). It stands between Main Street above and the Road below, with the tail race passing beside it at the upper left and the head race leaving it to the lower right, running down to a mill pond on the Musconetcong River. The D.L.&W. railroad crosses the top of the inset on a bridge over the tail race. The inset carries its own scale note and a north arrow. It repeats, in more detail, the mill buildings drawn at the centre of the main part of the sheet.
notes: No street junction is drawn here; the part is placed by three corners of the mill building carried from the main part (sheet-21-1), with scale 8.08 px/ft and north at -106 degrees. Low confidence; the carried points depend on the placement of the main part, which rests on one point.
The mills' building outlines measure the same on both parts (about 50 ft and 85 ft between the chosen corners).

sheet-22-1.description: The main map of sheet 22 lies in the lower right of the page and shows the southeastern edge of Washington borough, drawn at 100 ft to an inch. Railroad Avenue and Fisher Avenue run roughly north to south through the middle, with the short cross streets James and O'Shea Alley between them; County Road crosses the foot of the part on a slant. Between the two avenues the blocks are numbered 17, 56, 56 1/2 and 56 1/3. The northern edge is crossed by the D.L. & W. R.R. lines, labelled Phillipsburg Branch and Hampton Branch, and by the lines of the D.L. & W. R.R. Passenger Station, a pink and yellow building near the top right, with a large pink freight or storage building and a long yellow shed near the top. A dash-dot line labelled Borough Line crosses the part from lower left to upper right; the open ground south of it is lettered Washington Township, and only a few houses, hospital and chicken houses stand there. Dwellings of one and two storeys stand along the east side of Fisher Avenue and along Railroad Avenue north of the borough line, with 6 inch and 8 inch water pipes marked along James and Railroad Avenue and fire hydrants at corners. Street widths of 25 to 70 ft are lettered along the lines. A compass rose with a north arrow stands at the right. The lower left of the part continues to the left edge of the page below the Broadway inset, with the township ground and the Brooder house and chicken houses.
notes: Railroad Avenue, Fisher Avenue and James Street are Railroad Avenue, Fisher Avenue and James Street today; O'Shea Alley is Oshea Street.
County Road is not matched to Washburn Avenue: the modern road lies about 30 m from the drawn one, so it was left out of the control.

sheet-22-2.description: The top part of sheet 22 shows the hamlet of Broadway, headed 'Located 4 1/2 Miles W. of Washington', 'Not Incorporated', with a population of 200. It is a ribbon of settlement strung along the Morris Turnpike, which runs across the full width of the page. At the left edge Montana Road runs off to the north and Asbury Road to the south, and the Post Office stands at their corner on the south side. Along the turnpike are small frame dwellings and barns on long narrow lots, the M.E. Church with 'pipeless furnace, light elec.' near the middle, a public school, a garage, an auto dealer and 'Clarence Warne, Saw Mill and 2nd Hand Garage', with a sawmill and its boiler and engine, at the upper right. A further garage with a tile building stands at the right edge. House numbers 101 to 195 run along the north side and 144 to 192 on the south, and block numbers 207 and 208 are printed in the lots. A lane runs south from the turnpike near the centre. Notes at the top give the local conditions: water facilities none, fire department none, and the turnpike concrete paved with light grades. A north arrow at about 18 degrees stands in the middle. The part is drawn at 100 ft to an inch, and its lower edge is the heavy line that separates it from the inset and from the Washington map below.
notes: Morris Turnpike is West Washington Avenue (NJ 57) today, Montana Road is Millbrook Road, and Asbury Road is Asbury-Broadway Road.

sheet-23-1.description: The lower part of sheet 23 shows the centre of the hamlet of New Village, 'Located 6 1/2 Miles W. of Washington', with a population of 350, drawn at 100 ft to an inch. The Morris Turnpike crosses the lower third from left to right. North Thatcher Avenue runs up the page from the turnpike to 2nd Street, and Thatcher Avenue continues south of it to 3rd Street; Edison Road runs along the right side, marked North Edison Road above the turnpike and Edison Road below it, with its two parts offset at the crossing. Cross streets are 2nd Street and 3rd Street. The blocks are numbered 209, 210, 214, 215, 216, 217 and 219 and 220. Buildings are mostly detached frame dwellings with barns and sheds, a Public School of one storey (heat furnace, no light) south of the turnpike, a slaughter house on the west side of Thatcher Avenue, and, at the upper left, the premises of August Bevilacqua with a slaughter house and cold storage under construction. The dry bed of the former Morris Canal crosses the upper part of the area as two long curved lines and a road crosses it on a bridge at the left. A compass rose and north arrow stand at the right, with the scale bar at the lower left. The upper edge of the part is the heavy dividing line that zigzags across the page.
notes: Morris Turnpike is West Washington Avenue today; the other streets keep their names (Thatcher Avenue, 2nd Street, 3rd Street, Edison Road).
An unnamed road lettered only 'Road' joins the dry canal bed at the left and was not used.
Fitted scale is 4.2 px/ft, about 4 percent above the nominal 100 ft scan scale.

sheet-23-2.description: The upper part of sheet 23 shows the western end of New Village along the Morris Turnpike, which runs straight across the top of the page. Stewartsville Road leaves the turnpike at the left of centre and runs south-west, past the former public school, which is marked closed, toward the lower left corner. Ridgewood Avenue and Belvidere Road run off to the north from the turnpike, with a broad lot pattern behind the houses. A stream, drawn in blue, comes down from the turnpike near the centre, passes under a culvert and runs south toward the heavy dividing line. House numbers run along the turnpike and Stewartsville Road. Near the right is the Union Chapel in pink brick, and nearby is the Franklin House, a long hotel or boarding building. Most of the other buildings are frame dwellings, barns and sheds on large lots; a few of the stable and shop buildings are shaded blue, meaning iron or stone clad. Block numbers 209 to 213 are printed in the open ground. The notes at the right give the village as 'Located 6 1/2 Miles W. of Washington', population 350, not incorporated, water facilities none, fire department none, with the nearest assistance at Phillipsburg about 4 miles distant. The north arrow is about 18 degrees, and the lower boundary of the part is the heavy line that zigzags across the sheet.
notes: Morris Turnpike is West Washington Avenue today and Stewartsville Road keeps its name. Ridgewood Avenue is not in the modern street data; Belvidere Road could not be matched to the modern road of the same name.

sheet-24-1.description: Sheet 24 shows the works of the Edison Portland Cement Co. at New Village, drawn at 100 ft to an inch, 'About 1 mile' from the village. The main part of the sheet is the plant itself, a long north-south chain of buildings joined by conveyors, which runs down the centre of the page. At the top are the cement stock houses numbers 1 and 2, with the packing houses and the Bag Service Co. building; the middle holds the fine grinding, clinker stock house, dryer and coal buildings and the large roasting house with ten rotary kilns; and the lower part holds the chalk stock house, the new stock house, chalk grinding, the rock dryers, the long rock stock house and the train shed. On the left are the laboratory, hospital, machine shop, store room, carpenter shop, a cooling basin and a blue stream, with the Phillipsburg Branch of the D.L. & W. R.R., a passenger station and a freight house on the left side. 'Road to New Village' runs in from the upper left and crosses the tracks. Most buildings are marked as iron with wood scaffolding, and the notes describe a private water system, two reservoirs and the plant's fire protection. A compass rose stands at the right of the plant, with the north arrow turned about 45 degrees to the left of the page. Three boxes set apart by heavy lines in the upper left and right corners are separate parts.
notes: Road to New Village is Edison Road today.
